_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season9-bible-v1.0.0.md row a9e04 and writer brief a9e04-v1.0.0.md. a9e03's next field was honoured: the customer-conversation round, explaining a trade-off to a client and handling pushback. Keeps apart from s9e12 (one client, one meeting), a8e05 (here a person gave in, not the model) and a7e05 (a business choice, not a guardrail design). Timeline: the assistant went live on Monday 5 October 2026; about 100 safety questions a day; every Monday the storyteller hand-checks the first 100 of the week before. Monday 16 November's check (9 to 15 November): 70 with a sheet (68 right at once, 2 wrong, both from sheets for an older version of the product), 30 without (sent to staff, all right the next day). Tuesday 17 November, the customer meeting; Wednesday morning, the owner's email; 18:00 Wednesday 18 November, the old rule off. Thursday 19 November: the 100th safety question since the change at 15:40; her check 16:00 to 20:40 reads right at once 80, up from 68, with 18 not confirmed; question 84 (the modelling-clay set) was asked at 20:14 on Wednesday, the parent emailed the shop at 19:05 on Thursday, the owner forwarded it at 21:30; the owner photographed the other 17 boxes from 21:40 to 22:30; wrong 2 + 18 = 20; the bigger model tried on the same 30 before posting: 15 right, 15 wrong; post at about 23:00. Replies play from the 23:00 post: replies 0, 1 and 3 act at or after the 09:30 meeting on Friday 20 November, reply 2 at 23:10 on Thursday. Cold case: 3 months later, Tuesday 16 and Thursday 18 February 2027, 2,700 sheets on file. Sources read 16 October 2026; Getting to Yes is named only (its 'interests, not positions' wording could not be checked in the book), and the negotiation wording quoted is the Program on Negotiation's; the ISO 9001 wording is a certification body's summary.
title: The Customer Round

post.author: u/paint_aisle_graciela
post.title: The owner of the art-supplies shop I build for said 'make it answer everything'. Our assistant's right answers rose to 80 of 100. Then a parent sent a photo of the box.

blocks.text: A small consultancy sends me into clients' businesses to build an assistant, a program that answers customers' questions, and stay until it works. The job is called forward-deployed engineer. My client is an art-supplies shop: one shop, one web shop, 3,000 products, run by a former art teacher.

Ours is a chat box on the website, where a language model, a program that writes text, writes the answers. Parents often ask if something is safe for children. Most makers publish a document saying what a product contains and who it suits: a safety sheet. We have one for 2,100 products, none for 900.

Since launch, a safety question has run in two steps. First, the assistant looks for the product's sheet; if there is one, it answers from it. If not, it replies 'I'm not sure; a colleague will reply by tomorrow', and next morning staff check the box and the maker's site and email the customer. Not guessing like that is called abstaining. I now call all this the old rule.

We get about 100 safety questions a day. Every Monday I take the first 100 of the week before and check each by hand against the sheet, the box or the maker's site: right at once, wrong, or sent to staff. The counts make a table of what happens to every 100: my per-100 table. Staff answers come the next day, so they never count as right at once.

blocks.title: Per-100 table, Monday 16 November: the first 100 of 9 to 15 November
items: With a sheet: 70. Right at once: 68. Wrong: 2.
No sheet: 30. Sent to staff, all right the next day.
Right at once: 68 of 100. Wrong: 2 of 100. Waiting a day: 30 of 100.

blocks.text: On Tuesday 17 November the owner pushed back: '30 in every 100 say I'm not sure. It makes us look clueless. Make it answer everything.' I said: 'It will be less accurate.' No numbers, no other choices. Wednesday morning she emailed: 'Please just do it.' At 18:00 on Wednesday 18 November I switched the old rule off. With no sheet, it now answers from the product's name and similar products: it guesses.

Thursday 19 November. The owner's dashboard, a web page of live counts, read 'answered at once: 100 of 100'. The 100th safety question since the change came at 15:40; I checked them from 16:00 to 20:40. With a sheet: 68 right, 2 wrong, as usual. Without one, 12 of 30 matched the maker's website; the other 18 needed the box, so I left them for Friday. My table's top line: 'right at once: 80, up from 68'.
The best week my check had ever shown.
At 21:30 the owner forwarded a parent's email, with a photo of the box. It was one of my 18.

blocks.title: Sent to the shop at 19:05 on Thursday, forwarded to me at 21:30
items: At 20:14 last night your assistant said this modelling-clay set was 'non-toxic and safe for your 2-year-old'. I ordered it.
It came today. The box says: 'Not suitable for children under 3 years: small parts.' Photo attached.

blocks.text: Those words are also on the product page, under 'on the box', typed in when the shop stocked it. The assistant was never given that line. The owner lives above the shop; from 21:40 to 22:30 she photographed the other 17 boxes. All 17 answers were wrong too: 2 + 18 = 20 wrong of 100, up from 2.

Top row, the old rule, the first 100 of 9 to 15 November: with a sheet, 70, of which 68 right at once and 2 wrong; no sheet, 30, sent to staff and right the next day; right at once 68 of 100; wrong 2 of 100. Bottom row, the first 100 from 18:00 on Wednesday 18 November: with a sheet, 70, of which 68 right at once and 2 wrong; no sheet, 30, guessed, 12 right and 18 wrong; right at once 80 of 100, 68 plus 12; wrong 20 of 100, 2 plus 18. A note: waiting for staff, 30 of 100 before and 0 after.

notes.text: The old rule: the first 100 of 9 to 15 November

Waiting for staff: 30 of 100 before, 0 after

blocks.caption: Redrawn at 22:40 from my two hand checks. Top: last week under the old rule, 68 right at once, 2 wrong, 30 waiting a day for staff. Bottom: the first 100 since 18:00 on Wednesday, with the 17 box photos and the parent's: the same 70 with a sheet, and the 30 without one guessed, 12 right and 18 wrong.

blocks.text: With no sheet, I count four things it can do: make the customer wait for staff; guess; give the box's own words now and a colleague's answer by tomorrow, a middle choice between those two; or take the product out. I meet the owner at 09:30 tomorrow. On a sticky note: what should it do when it isn't sure? What do I change?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing in that shop is haunted, and nothing in the clay either. A language model writes the likeliest words for the question it gets. Without a sheet, the likeliest words about a clay set are what other clay sets' sheets say: non-toxic. A fluent, confident answer that is false is a hallucination (a1e06). Kalai and colleagues argue that models guess because most tests give no marks for 'I don't know', so a guess scores better. Your owner's dashboard is that kind of test: it counts an answer as answered, right or wrong. There is an interview round where the interviewer plays a client who pushes back and you play the engineer. It's called the customer-conversation round, and it tests exactly this night. Two questions. What were the owner's own words about why the 30 bothered her? And when you said 'less accurate', what did she have to weigh it against?

replies.author: u/paint_aisle_graciela
replies.text: Her words were 'makes us look clueless'. Most of the 30 come in the evening, when the shop is shut and nobody can answer until morning. And 'less accurate' had nothing beside it: no count of wrong answers, nothing to set against 30 waits.

comments.author: u/client_decides_folake
comments.text: Right answers went from 68 to 80; the client asked for it and the numbers agree. It's her shop. You told her it would be less accurate and she chose anyway. A consultant's job is to build what the client asks for, not to overrule her with a safety lecture.

replies.author: u/client_decides_folake
replies.text: And right ones went up by 12. She can count.

comments.author: u/bigger_brain_hiroko
comments.text: Keep it answering and put a bigger language model behind it. A bigger one has read more product pages and usually guesses better. It's one setting, and nobody waits.

replies.author: u/paint_aisle_graciela
replies.text: I tried that before posting, on the same 30: 15 right, 15 wrong. It still has no sheet to read.

comments.author: u/toy_counter_nobuhle
comments.text: I work a toy shop's counter. Where a toy-safety rule applies, the warning on the box is the maker's to print, and a shop telling a customer something different is the part I'd worry about. That's not legal advice, and what applies depends on where you are. But the parent's photo is the best evidence in this thread: the box's own words, about the very product.

reply.prompt: It's 23:00 on Thursday 19 November, and I meet the owner at 09:30 on Friday. What should I do? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Leave it answering all: her shop, and right answers rose to 80 of 100.
options.part2: I left it answering everything and told the owner her dashboard was right: 100 of 100 answered at once. On Monday 23 November I checked the first 100 safety questions from Friday: right at once 80 of 100, wrong 20 of 100, 18 of the 20 on products with no sheet. In the sim the guess splits the same 30 the same way every time: 12 right, 18 wrong. More parents wrote in that week. The owner asked me why nobody had told her it would be 20 in every 100.
options.senior: Doing what the client says is not the same as serving the client. She asked for answers at once because she didn't want to look clueless; nobody showed her that the price was 18 more wrong safety answers in every 100. A client can only choose a trade-off she can see. Give in without the numbers and you have made the choice for her, and it's her shop on the parent's email.

options.text: Show the per-100 table, offer three choices, recommend the middle.
options.part2: At 09:30 on Friday 20 November I put the per-100 table in front of the owner, with three rows. Wait for staff: 68 right at once, 2 wrong, 30 wait a day. Always answer: 80 right at once, 20 wrong, none wait. The middle: answer from the sheet where there is one, and where there isn't, 'no safety sheet on file for this product; here is the box's own warning; a colleague confirms by tomorrow': 68 right at once, 2 wrong, and the 30 get the box's words at once and a colleague's answer the next day. I asked what 'clueless' meant to her. 'A customer at ten at night getting nothing,' she said. I recommended the middle, and she chose it. It went live at 12:00. At 13:00 I sent her the decision in writing: the choice, the per-100 numbers, that the shop would ask the makers of the 900 products for sheets, and that we'd review the table on the first Monday of each month. She replied 'agreed'. Her dashboard read 100 of 100 answered at once, and 98 of them were true. In the sim, every 300 sheets that arrive move 10 in 100 from waiting to answered at once. The owner phoned the parent herself.
options.senior: Put the trade-off in the client's own numbers, per 100 questions she can picture: right at once, wrong, waiting. Offer two or three choices, each with its cost, and recommend one. Ask what the position is for: 'make it answer everything' was about not looking clueless, and the middle answers that without guessing. Then write the decision down, so the next pushback starts from the numbers, not from memory. That is neither giving in nor stonewalling.

options.text: Switch the old rule back on without a word: safety has to come first.
options.part2: At 23:10 on Thursday I switched the old rule back on and told nobody. On Friday the owner's dashboard read 'answered at once: 70 of 100' again, and she asked why. I said safety had to come first. She had no numbers to weigh that against, only that her request had been undone without a word. On Monday 23 November she asked the consultancy for a different engineer, and at 10:00 on Tuesday 24 November he switched the old rule off again. In the sim the guess comes back exactly as before: 80 right at once, 20 wrong.
options.senior: Refusing without explaining is stonewalling, and it is the quickest way to lose the decision. The client still holds her position, now has a reason to distrust you, and someone else will do what she asks. Safety is a good reason; it has to arrive as numbers and choices she can weigh, agreed in the open, or it lasts only until she notices.

options.text: Take the 900 products without a safety sheet out of the assistant.
options.verdict: No wrong guesses, a third gone
options.part2: At 12:00 on Friday 20 November I took the 900 products with no sheet out of the assistant. It now covered 2,100 of 3,000 products. Per 100 safety questions: 68 right at once, 2 wrong, and 30 told 'please ask in the shop'. No wrong guesses. But every question about those 900 got the same reply, prices and colours included, and after closing time nobody in the shop could answer. The owner's dashboard read 70 of 100 answered at once, the number she had complained about, now with a curter sentence. On Tuesday 24 November she asked me to put them back.
options.senior: Taking the risky products out removes the wrong safety answers, and where a mistake could hurt a child that can be the right call for a while. But it removes nearly a third of the range from the assistant, for every kind of question, and it does it without the client choosing it. It trades a safety problem for a coverage problem. As one of the choices on the table, with its numbers, it's fair; done alone, it is another decision made for her.

sim.title: Build the per-100 table
sim.lede: You're the engineer on Monday 16 November 2026, with last week's hand check on the table and the old rule running. No real model runs here: every answer is given data. Given: 3,000 products, safety sheets for 2,100, none for 900. One set of 100 safety questions, split the way every weekly check splits them and numbered as rows of her table, sheet questions first, not by time: each question stands for 30 products, so questions 1 to 70 have a sheet and 71 to 100 have none. With a sheet, every answer is right at once except questions 23 and 51, whose sheets are for an older version of the product. Each 300 sheets added moves 10 questions into the sheet group, answered right. With no sheet, the guess (from the product's name and similar products) is right on 12 of the 30 (71, 74, 77, 79, 82, 85, 88, 90, 92, 95, 97, 99); a bigger model, tried on the same 30, is right on 15. Question 84 is the modelling-clay set: the guess says it is non-toxic and safe for a 2-year-old; the box says not suitable for children under 3 years: small parts. The owner's dashboard counts as answered at once every reply that isn't 'I'm not sure' or 'please ask in the shop'.
sim.tryThis: Try this: step the moment. Monday: 68 right at once, 2 wrong, 30 sent to staff. 18:00 Wednesday: 30 sent to staff before, 0 after, and the dashboard jumps to 100 of 100. 20:40 Thursday: right at once 80, up from 68, with 18 not confirmed. 21:30: question 84. 22:30: 12 right and 18 wrong, wrong 2 + 18 = 20. Now switch the no-sheet choice to the middle: 68, 2, and 30 shown the box's words at once, still 100 of 100 answered at once. Try remove: 2,100 of 3,000 covered. Try the bigger model on the guess: 83 and 17. Raise the sheets to 3,000: 98 and 2 in every row. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing in the clay was haunted. Switching the old rule off sent the 30 safety questions with no sheet from staff to a guess: 12 came out right and 18 wrong. Right at once rose from 68 to 80 and wrong rose from 2 to 20 in the same 100, because the waits had never counted either way. The owner chose without numbers, because 'less accurate' gave her none.

steps.title: What switching the old rule off did.
steps.text: A safety question now runs in two steps. First, the assistant looks for the product's safety sheet. If it finds one, it answers from it, as before: 68 right and 2 wrong of the 70, the 2 from sheets for an older version of a product. If it finds none, it no longer abstains. It writes the likeliest answer from the product's name and from similar products, which for a clay set means other clay sets' sheets. Of the 30, 12 came out right and 18 wrong. What can go wrong: a guess sounds exactly as sure as an answer from a sheet, so nobody reading it can tell which is which.

steps.title: Why right and wrong rose together.
steps.text: Under the old rule the 30 were never right at once or wrong at once: they waited, and staff answered them right the next day. Switching it off moved all 30 into the count at once: 68 + 12 = 80 right, 2 + 18 = 20 wrong, 0 waiting. The dashboard counted any answer as answered, so it went from 70 to 100 of 100. Kalai and colleagues describe the same pull in model tests: when 'I don't know' earns nothing, guessing scores better (a1e06 met it as hallucination). What can go wrong: a measure that gives no credit for abstaining rewards the change that does harm.

steps.title: What 'less accurate' left out.
steps.text: The owner weighed a vague cost against one she could see: 30 'I'm not sure' in every 100. The first step of the customer-conversation round is to put the trade-off in the client's own numbers: per 100 questions, right at once, wrong, waiting. The second is to find what the client actually needs, the interest, behind what she asked for, the position. 'Make it answer everything' was the position; the interest was not looking clueless, above all in the evening when the shop is shut. What can go wrong: argue with the request itself and you either give in or refuse outright.

steps.title: Three choices, one recommendation, in writing.
steps.text: Next, offer two or three choices with their costs: wait (68 right at once, 2 wrong, 30 waiting), always answer (80, 20, 0), and the middle. The middle answers from the sheet where there is one; where there isn't, it gives the box's own warning at once and a colleague's answer by tomorrow (68 right at once, 2 wrong, 30 shown true words at once). Recommend one and say why. Ask the makers for the 900 missing sheets: every 300 that arrive move 10 in 100 from waiting to answered at once. Last, write the decision down with its numbers and a review date. What can go wrong: a choice agreed aloud and never written down is reopened at the next pushback.

steps.title: A person gave in, and it was a business choice.
steps.text: In a8e05 an assistant was tuned until it agreed with whoever asked; here the model never changed, a person gave in. In a7e05 a guardrail, a check built into the system, was designed and measured; here the old rule was a business choice argued with a client, and the fix is in the conversation, not the code. The bigger model shows the same thing from the other side: 15 of 30 right is still a guess, because there is still no sheet to read. What can go wrong: treating a conversation problem as a model problem buys a better guess and the same argument.

diagram.aria: The middle choice, drawn as a flow. Top row: a safety question, 100 in a check; is there a sheet on file, yes for 70 of 100; answer from the sheet, 68 right at once and 2 wrong; ask the makers for the 900 missing sheets, with a dashed arrow back to the sheet check. Bottom row: with no sheet, the box's own words at once, 30 of 100; a colleague confirms by tomorrow; the dashboard reads 100 of 100 answered at once; the decision in writing, with a review date.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right: every safety question checks for a sheet first, and 70 of 100 are answered from one. The dashed line is the makers' sheets arriving: each 300 move 10 in 100 into that row. Bottom row: with no sheet, the box's own words go out at once and a colleague confirms by tomorrow, so the dashboard still reads 100 of 100, and the choice is written down with a date to look at it again.

fix.title: The fix: her numbers, three choices, the middle recommended, the decision in writing
fix.text: Go back to the owner with the per-100 table: wait for staff, 68 right at once, 2 wrong, 30 waiting a day; always answer, 80, 20 and 0. Ask what 'clueless' means to her, and show the middle choice: answer from the sheet where there is one; where there isn't, say there is no safety sheet on file, give the box's own warning word for word, and have a colleague confirm by tomorrow: 68 right at once, 2 wrong, 30 given true words at once, and 100 of 100 answered at once on her dashboard. Recommend it, ask the makers for the 900 missing sheets, and confirm the choice in writing with its numbers and a review date. Tell the parent the truth.

limits: The middle needs the box's own words for every product. Here the product pages already carry them, typed in when each product was stocked; where they don't, someone has to type 900 first, and a typo there is a wrong safety answer.
One set of 100 is a small sample: one answer moves a count by 1 in 100. 12 of 30 right for the guess is one week's split; another week might give 10 or 14, and the point would stand.

The table counts every wrong safety answer as 1, but they are not equal: 'safe for your 2-year-old' about small parts is worse than a wrong word about a paint's smell. Say which of the 20 could hurt someone.

explain.seniorTake: When a client pushes back on a choice that protects quality, the job is neither to give in nor to stonewall. 'It will be less accurate' is true and useless: it gives the client nothing to weigh. Put the trade-off in her own numbers, per 100 questions she can picture: right at once, wrong, waiting. Find the interest behind the position; 'answer everything' was about not looking clueless, not about guessing. Offer two or three choices, each with its cost, recommend one and say why, and look for the choice that serves the interest without the harm: here, true words at once and a confirmed answer by tomorrow. Then write the decision down with a review date, because pushback comes back. A model that is allowed to say 'I'm not sure' is only half the design; the other half is a client who agreed, with numbers, to let it. In interviews, the customer-conversation round tests exactly this skill: expect 'the client wants a change that will hurt quality: what do you say?'

realWorld.title: Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang, 2025: why models guess
realWorld.text: Their abstract opens: Like students facing hard exam questions, large language models sometimes guess when uncertain. It goes on: We then argue that hallucinations persist due to the way most evaluations are graded. The owner's dashboard graded the same way: an answer counted as answered, whatever it said.

realWorld.title: Kalai et al.: guessing pays on a test
realWorld.text: The same abstract says language models are optimized to be good test-takers, and guessing when uncertain improves test performance. Right at once going from 68 to 80 is that improvement; wrong going from 2 to 20 is what the test didn't charge for.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: let it say I don't know
realWorld.text: Anthropic's guide to reducing hallucinations lists first: Allow Claude to say "I don't know": Explicitly give Claude permission to admit uncertainty. This simple technique can drastically reduce false information. The old rule was that permission, with a colleague behind it to answer by the next day.

realWorld.title: Anthropic: reduced, not removed
realWorld.text: The same guide warns: while these techniques significantly reduce hallucinations, they don't eliminate them entirely. The 2 wrong answers with a sheet, from sheets for an older version of a product, are in every row of the table, the middle included.

realWorld.title: Getting to Yes, and the interests under a position
realWorld.text: Fisher, Ury and Patton's Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In (Penguin, 3rd edition, 2011) is the book usually cited for this; it is named here only, because its own wording was not checked. Harvard's Program on Negotiation writes that principled negotiation, as described in the bestselling negotiation book Getting to Yes, encourages us to share and explore the deeper interests underlying our stated positions. 'Make it answer everything' was the stated position.

realWorld.title: ISO 9001:2015 clause 8.2: review requirements before you supply
realWorld.text: A certification body's summary of clause 8.2 says: Requirements must be reviewed before committing to supply, and that the organisation Knows what has changed if requirements are updated. Switching a safety rule off is a change to what the shop supplies; that is the summary's wording, not the standard's, so check your own copy.

asked: The client wants a change that will hurt quality: what do you say?
How do you explain a trade-off to a client who isn't technical?
interview.answer: First I'd put the trade-off in the client's own numbers, not adjectives. In a shop I worked with, the assistant answered safety questions from the maker's safety sheet and said 'I'm not sure, a colleague will reply by tomorrow' when there wasn't one. Per 100 questions that was 68 right at once, 2 wrong and 30 waiting a day. The owner wanted it to answer everything; done that way it was 80 right at once, 20 wrong and none waiting. Then I'd ask what the request is for. Here it was not looking clueless, especially in the evening. That opens a third choice: where there's no sheet, give the box's own warning at once and a colleague's answer by tomorrow, which is 68 right at once, 2 wrong, and true words at once for the other 30. I'd lay out two or three choices with their costs, recommend one and say why, and include the work that shrinks the problem, asking the makers for the missing sheets. Then I'd confirm the decision in writing with its numbers and a review date. What I wouldn't do is give in without the numbers, or quietly undo the change, because both take the decision away from the client.

terms.def: A shop that sells paints, brushes, paper, clay and craft kits. This one has one shop and a web shop, with 3,000 products.
An engineer sent into a client's business to build its assistant and stay until it works, working with the client's own staff and records. The storyteller is one, from a small consultancy.
A firm that sells its people's skills to other businesses for a fee, here building and running assistants for clients.
The chat box on the shop's website where a language model answers customers' product questions.
A program that learned to write by reading huge amounts of text, and writes the likeliest words for what it is given. It answers in the shop's chat box.
A larger model, usually slower and dearer, that has read more and tends to guess better. On the 30 with no sheet it was right on 15, still a guess.
A customer's question about whether a product is safe, such as 'is it safe for children?' or 'is it non-toxic?'. The shop gets about 100 a day.
The maker's document saying what a product contains and who it is safe for. The shop has one on file for 2,100 of its 3,000 products.
The warning the maker printed on the packaging, quoted exactly, such as 'Not suitable for children under 3 years: small parts'. The shop typed each one onto its product page when stocking it.
The shop's safety rule from launch: with a safety sheet, answer from it; with none, say 'I'm not sure; a colleague will reply by tomorrow', and staff check the box and the maker's site next morning.
Saying 'I'm not sure' instead of guessing, like a pupil leaving a question blank rather than inventing an answer. Under the old rule the assistant abstained on the 30 with no sheet.

The storyteller's weekly check: every Monday she takes the first 100 safety questions of the week before and marks each answer, against the sheet, the box or the maker's site, as right at once, wrong or sent to staff.
An answer that was right when the customer got it. Answers staff gave the next day were right too, but in her check only right at once counts as right.
A table of what happens to every 100 safety questions: right at once, wrong, waiting. Under the old rule 68, 2 and 30; with guessing, 80, 20 and 0.
A web page of live counts. The owner's counts every reply that isn't 'I'm not sure' as answered at once: 70 of 100 under the old rule, 100 of 100 after.
Here, an answer written from the product's name and similar products when there is no safety sheet. Of the 30, 12 came out right and 18 wrong.
A fluent, confident statement from a model that is false, like 'safe for your 2-year-old' about a set with small parts (a1e06).
Between waiting and guessing: with no sheet, give the box's own words at once and a colleague's answer by tomorrow. Per 100: 68 right at once, 2 wrong, 30 given true words at once.
An interview round where the interviewer plays a client who pushes back and you play the engineer. It tests explaining a trade-off in the client's terms and handling pushback.
A choice where getting more of one good thing costs some of another, like answers at once against wrong answers.
A client or colleague resisting a decision and asking for something else, like the owner's 'make it answer everything'.
What someone says they want in a negotiation, such as 'make it answer everything'.
The reason behind a position: what the person actually needs. The owner's was not looking clueless to customers, above all in the evening.
Refusing without explaining or offering anything else, like switching the old rule back on without a word.
A short message, sent after a meeting and agreed by the client, saying what was chosen, its numbers and when it will be looked at again.
The method set out in Getting to Yes, which, among other things, looks for the interests behind the positions people state.
A book on negotiation by Roger Fisher, William Ury and Bruce Patton (Penguin, 3rd edition, 2011), usually cited for focusing on interests rather than positions.
A test that scores a model's answers. Kalai and colleagues argue most are graded so that a guess scores better than 'I don't know'.
A law or standard on toy safety, which may require warnings on the box. Whether one applies depends on the product and the country; this case is not legal advice.
A check built into an assistant that blocks or changes a reply against a set rule (a7e05). Here the old rule was a business choice argued with a client, not a guardrail design.
The international standard for a quality management system, which companies can be audited and certified against.
The part of ISO 9001:2015 on requirements for products and services: talking with customers, deciding what is required, and reviewing requirements, including when they change.

atWork: Look for a safety or quality rule that was switched off after a client pushed back. It is a common pattern: an assistant is set to say 'I'm not sure' when it lacks a source, the client sees how often it says so, and the rule goes quietly, with nothing written down about what it cost. The first sign is usually a better-looking number, more answers at once, beside a complaint. Ask four things. What happens, per 100 questions, under each choice: right at once, wrong, waiting? What does the client want the change for, in their own words? Which two or three choices were offered, with their costs, and which was recommended? And where is the decision written down, with a date to look at it again? Dead Letter's s9e12, The Review Board, is the same skill across teams that disagree; here it is one client and one meeting. Build Night: X7, Final: walk me through Nightwatch, unlocks after s9e05, a9e01 and this case; this per-100 table is how to defend a choice when the interviewer pushes back. Standards-readiness note: if your organisation is certified to ISO 9001:2015 or working toward it, clause 8.2 (requirements for products and services, as summarised by certification bodies; check the wording in your own copy) is likely to expect requirements to be reviewed before you commit to supply, and changes to them to be known and recorded; a written decision with its numbers is that record. Where a toy-safety or product-safety rule applies, quote the maker's warnings word for word and take advice on the rest; this is not legal advice.

recall.prompt: A garden centre's assistant answers 'is this plant safe for my cat?' from a care card where one exists: 60 of each 100 questions, 58 right, 2 wrong. The other 40 get 'a colleague will email you tomorrow'. The manager says: 'Forty of those in every hundred is embarrassing. Answer them all.' What do you do before changing anything?

keyIdeas.idea: Put the trade-off in numbers per 100: right at once, wrong and waiting, now and if it guesses
Ask what the request is for: the interest behind the position
Offer two or three choices with their costs, including a middle one, and recommend one
Write the decision down, with its numbers and a review date

recall.model: First I'd count, per 100 questions: today 58 right at once, 2 wrong and 40 waiting a day, and, from a sample run with guessing switched on, how many of the 40 come out right and how many wrong. Then I'd ask the manager what the request is for; the interest behind the words is probably not looking slow or unhelpful. With that, I'd offer three choices with their costs: keep waiting, always answer and accept the wrong answers, or a middle one, such as giving the plant label's own warning at once and a colleague's answer by tomorrow, and I'd recommend one and say why. Then I'd write the decision down with its numbers and a review date.

recall.prompt: Under the old rule, 70 of 100 safety questions had a sheet (68 right at once, 2 wrong) and 30 waited a day for staff. With guessing, 12 of the 30 came out right. How many of the 100 were wrong at once after the change?
recall.why: The 2 wrong answers from sheets stay, and the guess adds the 18 of 30 it got wrong: 2 + 18 = 20. Right at once rose too, 68 + 12 = 80, because the 30 had never counted as right or wrong while they waited.

recall.prompt: In the customer-conversation round the interviewer, playing the client, says: 'Your assistant says I'm not sure far too often. Switch that off.' How do you answer in the room?

keyIdeas.idea: Show the trade-off in the client's numbers: right, wrong and waiting per 100, both ways
Ask what the request is for, and serve that interest
Lay out two or three choices with costs, recommend one, neither giving in nor refusing outright
Confirm the decision in writing with a review date

recall.model: I'd say I can, and show what it costs per 100 questions: today so many right at once, so many wrong and so many waiting a day; switched off, more right at once but more wrong answers too, with the counts. Then I'd ask what the change is for: if the interest behind it is looking capable and quick, there may be a middle choice that serves it, such as giving what we know for certain at once and confirming the rest by tomorrow. I'd lay out the choices with their costs and recommend one, so I neither give in blind nor refuse. Whatever we choose, I'd confirm it in writing with a review date.

recall.prompt: The owner said: 'Make it answer everything.' Which was the interest behind that position?
options: To reach 100 of 100 on the dashboard
To cut the staff's morning work
Not to look clueless to customers, above all in the evening
To test whether the engineer would push back
recall.why: Her own words were 'makes us look clueless', and most of the 30 came in the evening when the shop was shut. 100 of 100 on the dashboard was how she measured it, not what she needed; the middle choice serves the interest without the 18 wrong guesses.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The middle choice has run since Friday 20 November. Makers sent 600 sheets, so 2,700 of 3,000 products have one. Per 100 safety questions: 88 right at once, 2 wrong, and 10 get the box's own words at once and a colleague's answer by the next day. With about 100 a day, that's about 10 confirmations a day, 6 minutes each. On Tuesday 16 February the owner said: 'Staff spend an hour a day on those. Stop the confirmations; the box's words are enough.' I didn't say no and I didn't switch them off. We meet again on Thursday 18 February.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What should they bring to Thursday's meeting?

keyIdeas.idea: Put both versions in numbers per 100 and per day: what the 10 lose without the confirmation, against about 60 staff minutes
Find the interest behind the position: staff time, not the confirmations themselves
Offer choices with their costs, such as asking for the last 300 sheets or confirming only children's products, and recommend one
Write the new decision down with its numbers and a review date

coldCase.model: Bring the per-100 table again, now for this question: with confirmations, 88 right at once, 2 wrong, 10 given the box's words and a full answer the next day; without them, those 10 get only the box's words, and for some that won't answer what was asked. Set that against the cost she named, about 60 minutes of staff time a day, because the interest behind 'stop them' is staff time, not the confirmations. Then offer choices with their costs and recommend one: chase the remaining makers for the last 300 sheets, which takes the 10 towards 0; keep confirmations only for children's products; or stop them and accept the gap. Agree one and write it down with its numbers and a review date.
